brief.topic: How a Grid Can Find One Broken Bit

s01: One tiny bit changes during a message.
Can the message tell us exactly where?
Arrange the bits in a grid.
Add one extra bit to each row, so the number of ones is even.
Then do the same for each column.
These extra bits are a small amount of deliberate redundancy.
Now flip this bit from zero to one.
Its row has an odd number of ones.
So does its column.
Every other row and column still passes the check.
Follow the failed row and the failed column.
Their crossing locates the changed bit.
Flip it back, and both checks become even again.
We found the error without keeping a second copy of the whole message.
This demonstration assumes exactly one data bit changed and the check bits arrived intact.
More errors need more care.
Watch four bits at the corners of a rectangle change together.
Every affected row changes twice.
Every affected column changes twice.
All the parity checks still pass, even though the message is different.
Redundancy can reveal a mistake.
The pattern of redundancy decides which mistakes remain invisible.

scenes.narration:
One tiny bit changes during a message. Can the message tell us exactly where?

Arrange the bits in a grid. Add one extra bit to each row, so the number of ones is even. Then do the same for each column. These extra bits are a small amount of deliberate redundancy.

Now flip this bit from zero to one. Its row has an odd number of ones. So does its column. Every other row and column still passes the check.

Follow the failed row and the failed column. Their crossing locates the changed bit. Flip it back, and both checks become even again. We found the error without keeping a second copy of the whole message.

This demonstration assumes exactly one data bit changed and the check bits arrived intact. More errors need more care.

Watch four bits at the corners of a rectangle change together. Every affected row changes twice. Every affected column changes twice. All the parity checks still pass, even though the message is different.

Redundancy can reveal a mistake. The pattern of redundancy decides which mistakes remain invisible.
